meta.title: Daily Reflection Tree
meta.description: A deterministic end-of-day reflection tool traversing three psychological axes: Locus (Victim↔Victor), Orientation (Entitlement↔Contribution), and Radius (Self-Centric↔Altrocentric).

axis1.name: Locus
axis1.theory: Rotter (1954) Locus of Control + Dweck (2006) Growth Mindset

axis2.name: Orientation
axis2.theory: Organ (1988) OCB + Campbell et al. (2004) Psychological Entitlement

nodes.text:
Good evening.

Before you close this day, take 3 minutes to look at it — not to grade yourself, but to understand it a little better.

There are no right answers here. There's just honesty.
How would you describe today in one word?

options.label: Productive
Mixed
Tough
Frustrating

nodes.comment: Routes based on A1_OPEN answer — positive days to high-agency question, hard days to low-agency question

nodes.text: You said "{A1_OPEN}". When something went well today, what was behind it?

options.label: I had thought it through beforehand
I adjusted my approach when I saw something wasn't working
My team came through and I made sure they had what they needed
Things happened to fall into place — I got fortunate

nodes.text: You said "{A1_OPEN}". When things got hard, what did you find yourself doing?

options.label: Looking for what I could still control
Pushing through, even if it felt pointless
Wondering why this keeps happening to me
Waiting for the situation to change on its own

nodes.text: When you replay today, which of these feels most honest?

options.label: I made at least one decision I'm actually proud of
I can see where I had a choice — I just didn't take it
I mostly reacted to what was thrown at me
I'm not sure — today felt mostly out of my hands

nodes.comment: Routes based on accumulated axis1 signals after 2 questions

nodes.text: You stayed in the driver's seat today — or at least tried to. Agency doesn't mean everything goes right. It means you kept asking: "What can I do here?" That question is worth more than a perfect day.

Today pulled your attention outward — toward what others did, what went wrong, what you couldn't change. That's a real experience. But somewhere in today, there was a moment — however small — where you made a call. Even choosing your attitude in a hard conversation is a decision. That counts.

Now let's shift.

How you showed up is one thing. What you gave — and what you expected — is another.
Think of one interaction you had today — with a colleague, a manager, a client. What was mostly on your mind?

options.label: Whether I was delivering what I'd promised
Whether the other person had what they needed
Getting proper credit for what I'd done
Whether others were pulling their fair share

nodes.text: You were thinking about giving or delivering today. When you reflect on that, which is most true?

options.label: I stretched beyond my job description and it felt right
I kept my head down and did what was mine to do
I gave a lot — but honestly, I expected something back
I wasn't sure what I owed, so I did less than I could have

nodes.text: You were tracking recognition or fairness today. What happened with that?

options.label: I didn't get what I felt I deserved — and I'm still thinking about it
I got recognition — and I noticed how much I needed it
I didn't get it, but I shifted focus back to the work itself
I realized my expectation may not have been reasonable to begin with

nodes.text: When you helped someone today — or had the chance to — what was the thought underneath it?

options.label: They needed it, so I helped — simple as that
It was part of my job, but I tried to make it count
I wondered if it would be noticed or remembered
I honestly didn't find a moment to help anyone

nodes.comment: Routes based on accumulated axis2 signals after 2 questions

nodes.text: You were thinking more about what you could give than what you'd receive. That's a quiet kind of leadership — often invisible in the moment, but it shapes the room. People around contribution-oriented colleagues work differently. You may not see it, but it registers.

You spent some energy today tracking what was owed to you — recognition, effort, fairness. That's human. But here's a question worth sitting with: if you picture those interactions from the other side, what would they have seen? Not for guilt — just to see the full picture.

One last dimension.

You've looked at how you handled things, and what you gave. Now: how wide was your lens today?
When you think about today's biggest challenge, whose experience matters most to you right now?

options.label: Mine — it was my challenge to carry
My team's — we were all in it together
A specific colleague who had it harder than me
The people at the other end — customers, end users

nodes.text: Is there someone who was affected by what you went through today — even indirectly?

options.label: Probably, but I didn't think about them much
Yes — and I checked in on them
Yes — and I wish I had reached out
I honestly don't know — I was in my own head today

nodes.text: You were aware of others today. Did that awareness actually change what you did?

options.label: Yes — I made a decision I wouldn't have made thinking only of myself
It shaped my thinking, even if the action was the same
I was aware, but I was too stretched to act on it
Honestly, caring about others made today harder — I'm working through that

nodes.comment: Routes based on accumulated axis3 signals after 2 questions

nodes.text: You were thinking beyond yourself today — about a colleague, a team, the people at the other end of your work. That kind of awareness doesn't just make you a better colleague. It changes what the work means. The hardest days become bearable when they're in service of something larger than you.

Today, your frame was mostly your own — your stress, your challenge, your load. That's not wrong; sometimes a day just demands everything you have. But here's a thought: the days you'll remember as meaningful are often the ones where you solved something for someone else. What might tomorrow look like with a slightly wider lens?

Today you showed up {axis1_summary} on agency, {axis2_summary} on contribution, and {axis3_summary} on your radius of concern.

{summary_reflection}
See you tomorrow.

summary_reflections.internal|contribution|altro: You were in the driver's seat, focused on giving, and thinking beyond yourself. Days like this build something — in you and in everyone around you. Carry this forward.
summary_reflections.internal|contribution|self: You had agency and gave well today. Tomorrow: widen the lens just slightly. Someone nearby may be part of a story you haven't noticed yet.
summary_reflections.internal|entitlement|altro: You had agency and a wide view of others. There's a gap in the middle worth exploring: what happens when you shift some of that 'what do I deserve' energy toward 'what can I give'? The leverage tends to compound.
summary_reflections.internal|entitlement|self: You made things happen today. The next layer is asking what those things were *for*. Contribution without expectation runs on a completely different fuel source.
summary_reflections.external|contribution|altro: You gave and stayed aware of others, even on a day that didn't cooperate. That's the hardest version of showing up well. The sense of agency will return — it usually does when we stop waiting for it.
summary_reflections.external|contribution|self: You gave more than you felt in control of. That tension is real. Tomorrow, notice the small decisions — they're there even on the hardest days.
summary_reflections.external|entitlement|altro: Today felt out of your hands, and you were tracking what was owed — but you were still thinking about others. That wider view is something. Start there tomorrow, and the agency tends to follow.
summary_reflections.external|entitlement|self: Today was hard, and the frame stayed close. That happens to everyone. Tomorrow is a clean start — one small choice, one small act, and the day already looks different.
